name: Steampunk

card.summary: A retro-futuristic Victorian-inspired style of clothing, hair, makeup and accessories that people adopt to craft a distinctive personal look.
card.note: A style subculture rather than a treatment; tight-lacing corsets and costume gear carry ordinary comfort considerations.

quick.overview:
Steampunk is a science-fiction subgenre and aesthetic built on 19th-century steam-era machinery, and steampunk fashion is its look: Victorian-style garments mixed with brass goggles, gears and rugged or post-apocalyptic touches. People use it as a costume or lifestyle style to present a distinctive, handmade appearance.

The style grew from late-20th-century novels and spread through conventions, Etsy craft sellers and runway collections. It is a style choice, so its payoff is in presentation and personal identity rather than any measured physical change.
quick.how: Followers assemble outfits from corsets and waistcoats, long coats, bustled or bell skirts, top hats or bowlers, boots, pocket watches and goggles, often handmade or modified. Hair, makeup and jewelry are styled to match, and events and conventions are where full outfits are worn.
quick.risks: Steampunk is a low-risk style. Corsets worn tightly can be uncomfortable, and costume pieces such as heavy leather, brass and buckles are practical considerations for heat and movement.

lead: Steampunk is a science-fiction subgenre featuring retro-futuristic technology inspired by 19th-century steam-powered machinery, usually set in alternate Victorian or Edwardian worlds [1]. As an aesthetic subculture it covers art, clothing and performance in that style [1].

Steampunk fashion is its wearable form. It blends a romanticised Victorian view of science with 19th-century industrial elements and spans clothing, hairstyling, jewelry, body modification and makeup [2]. Typical pieces include corsets worn as outerwear, waistcoats, lab coats, long skirts with bustles, brass goggles, hats such as bowlers and pith helmets, and mechanical-looking jewelry [2].

People adopt the style to stand out and to look distinctive and handmade. The look has no fixed rules [1], and its influence has reached the runway: Christian Dior's John Galliano brought steampunk elements to a 2010 show [2].

angle.text: Steampunk is a clothing and styling choice. Wearers use corsets, vests, hats, goggles and themed hair and makeup to present a distinctive aesthetic.

infobox: Late-20th-century science fiction; term coined by K. W. Jeter in 1987
Corsets, waistcoats, brass goggles, top hats

paras: In a 1987 letter to Locus magazine, author K. W. Jeter suggested the name steampunk for a group of 19th-century-set novels by himself, Tim Powers and James Blaylock, as a counterpart to cyberpunk [1]. The label was applied retroactively to earlier works such as Jeter's Morlock Night (1979), which is also considered the first steampunk novel and the starting point of the fashion [1][2].

Steampunk grew alongside goth and punk scenes in the 1980s and 1990s [2]. In 2005 Kate Lambert founded Steampunk Couture, reportedly the first steampunk clothing company, and the first steampunk convention, SalonCon, followed in 2006 [2]. Between 2009 and 2011 the term became a common label for handmade goods on Etsy [1]. The Oxford Museum of the History of Science hosted the first major steampunk art exhibition in 2009 to 2010, with over 80,000 visitors [1].

Steampunk dress has no fixed rules and mixes Victorian pieces such as corsets, bustles, waistcoats and top hats with military or post-apocalyptic elements such as gas masks [1]. Brass goggles are the signature accessory [2]. Modern versions can be as casual as graphic tees or jeans with belts and holsters [2].
The aesthetic has strong ties to DIY craft, and enthusiasts modify modern objects with brass, wood and leather to give them a Victorian appearance [1].

Steampunk appears in film, television, photography and music, and in 2012 an episode of America's Next Top Model featured a steampunk-themed shoot [2]. The style began influencing mainstream fashion trends from about 2015 [2].

timeline.event: K. W. Jeter's Morlock Night published, considered the first steampunk novel [2].
